details.value: General sensory (with sympathetic fibers from the internal carotid plexus)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Anterior ethmoidal foramen (with the anterior ethmoidal artery and vein) -> anterior cranial fossa on the cribriform plate -> nasal slit beside the crista galli -> nasal cavity -> emerges between the nasal bone and the lateral process of the septal cartilage as the external nasal nerve

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Anterior ethmoidal cells and frontal sinus mucosa; anterosuperior nasal septum (medial internal nasal branches) and anterior lateral nasal wall (lateral internal nasal branches); skin of the dorsum, tip and ala of the nose (external nasal branch)

details.label: Branches
details.value: Anterior meningeal twigs to the dura of the anterior fossa, internal nasal branches (medial and lateral), external nasal branch

pearl: Anterior cranial fossa fractures through the cribriform plate injure this nerve with the olfactory fila, so anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea can come with numbness of the nasal tip; its internal nasal branches are the main sensory supply of Kiesselbach's area, which is why anterior nasal packing and cautery for epistaxis need topical anesthesia of the anterior septum.

name: Posterior ethmoidal nerve
function: Small, inconstant branch of the nasociliary nerve (V1) that passes through the posterior ethmoidal foramen to supply the posterior ethmoidal cells and the sphenoidal sinus.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Leaves the nasociliary nerve on the medial orbital wall -> posterior ethmoidal foramen (with the posterior ethmoidal artery and vein) -> mucosa of the posterior ethmoidal cells and sphenoidal sinus

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Mucous membrane of the posterior ethmoidal air cells and the sphenoidal sinus

details.label: Branches
details.value: Mucosal twigs only; does not reach the nasal cavity proper

pearl: Pain from sphenoid and posterior ethmoid sinusitis is referred through V1 to the vertex, retro-orbital region and occiput rather than to the cheek, and the posterior ethmoidal foramen lies only a few millimetres in front of the optic canal, the landmark that limits dissection of the medial orbital wall.

name: Nasopalatine nerve
function: Longest branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion (V2) that crosses the roof of the nasal cavity, runs down the septum and descends through the incisive canal to supply the anterior hard palate behind the incisors.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory (V2) with postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor and sympathetic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Pterygopalatine fossa -> sphenopalatine foramen into the nasal cavity -> across the roof below the sphenoid sinus -> forward and downward in a groove on the vomer and septal cartilage -> incisive canal and incisive fossa to the palate

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Mucosa of the posteroinferior nasal septum; mucoperiosteum of the anterior hard palate (premaxilla) and gingiva lingual to the incisors and canines

details.label: Branches
details.value: Septal branches; communicates with the greater palatine nerve in the incisive canal

pearl: A nasopalatine block through the incisive papilla anesthetizes the palatal gingiva of the six anterior teeth; nasopalatine duct (incisive canal) cysts are the most common non-odontogenic cyst of the jaws, a heart-shaped midline lucency between the maxillary central incisors with vital teeth.

name: Greater and lesser palatine nerves
function: Descending branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion (V2) that pass through the palatine canals: the greater palatine nerve supplies the hard palate, the lesser palatine nerves the soft palate and tonsil.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory (V2) with parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to palatine glands; the lesser palatine nerves also carry taste fibers from the soft palate that travel via the greater petrosal nerve to CN VII

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Pterygopalatine fossa -> greater palatine canal between the maxilla and the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone -> greater palatine foramen (medial to the 3rd molar) for the greater nerve and lesser palatine foramina in the pyramidal process for the lesser nerves

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Greater: mucoperiosteum of the hard palate and palatal gingiva back to the canine, plus posterior inferior lateral nasal branches to the inferior meatus and concha. Lesser: soft palate, uvula and palatine tonsil

details.label: Branches
details.value: Posterior inferior lateral nasal branches (greater), tonsillar branches (lesser); communication with the nasopalatine nerve in the incisive canal

pearl: The greater palatine foramen is the landmark for a greater palatine block (palatal mucosa of the molars and premolars) and for injecting the descending palatine artery in posterior epistaxis; it also carries the artery that is harvested with a palatal flap for cleft palate repair. Pain referred to the ear from the soft palate and tonsil travels on lesser palatine and glossopharyngeal fibers.

name: Superior alveolar nerves (posterior, middle, anterior)
function: Three branches of the maxillary nerve and its infraorbital continuation that form the superior dental plexus in the wall of the maxillary sinus and supply the maxillary teeth, gingiva and sinus mucosa.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Posterior: leaves V2 in the pterygopalatine fossa and enters the posterior superior alveolar foramina on the maxillary tuberosity. Middle (inconstant) and anterior: leave the infraorbital nerve in the infraorbital groove/canal and run in canals in the lateral and anterior walls of the maxillary sinus

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Posterior: maxillary molars (except the mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar), adjacent buccal gingiva, maxillary sinus mucosa. Middle: premolars and the mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar. Anterior: incisors and canine; a nasal branch to the anterior inferior nasal wall and floor

details.label: Branches
details.value: Dental and gingival branches via the superior dental plexus; the plexus also communicates with the greater palatine and nasopalatine nerves

pearl: Maxillary sinusitis and sinus carcinoma present as diffuse upper-tooth pain because these nerves run in the sinus wall, and conversely molar root infection perforates into the sinus. A posterior superior alveolar block numbs the molars but risks a pterygoid-plexus hematoma, and a Le Fort or orbital floor fracture causes numbness of the upper teeth through the infraorbital trunk.

name: Intermediate nerve (of Wrisberg)
function: Smaller, sensory and parasympathetic root of the facial nerve that leaves the brainstem between CN VII motor root and CN VIII, carrying taste, cutaneous sensation and preganglionic secretomotor fibers that become the greater petrosal nerve and chorda tympani.

details.label: Type
details.value: Special sensory (taste, geniculate ganglion), general sensory (external ear), preganglionic parasympathetic (superior salivatory nucleus)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Pontomedullary junction (cerebellopontine angle) between the facial motor root and the vestibulocochlear nerve -> internal acoustic meatus -> joins the motor root at the geniculate ganglion in the facial canal

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and soft palate; lacrimal, nasal, palatine, submandibular and sublingual glands; skin of the concha and posterior external acoustic meatus

details.label: Branches
details.value: Greater petrosal nerve (at the geniculate ganglion) and chorda tympani; its cell bodies sit in the geniculate ganglion and project to the nuclei of the solitary tract

pearl: Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) reactivates in this nerve's sensory territory: vesicles in the ear canal and on the auricle, facial palsy, loss of taste on the anterior tongue and often vertigo or hearing loss from adjacent CN VIII; treat with antivirals plus steroids. Its intracanalicular course explains why an acoustic neuroma or CPA surgery can cause dry eye and taste loss before facial weakness.

name: Caroticotympanic nerves
function: Postganglionic sympathetic twigs from the internal carotid plexus that pass through the wall of the carotid canal into the middle ear to join the tympanic plexus.

details.label: Type
details.value: Postganglionic sympathetic (superior cervical ganglion)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Internal carotid plexus in the carotid canal -> caroticotympanic canaliculi in the bone between the carotid canal and the tympanic cavity (with the caroticotympanic artery) -> tympanic plexus on the promontory

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Vasomotor fibers to the mucosa of the tympanic cavity, mastoid air cells and auditory tube; they travel with the tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve toward the otic ganglion and parotid

details.label: Branches
details.value: Superior and inferior caroticotympanic nerves joining the tympanic nerve of CN IX (Jacobson) and the lesser petrosal nerve

pearl: They are a reminder that the tympanic plexus mixes CN IX parasympathetic fibers with sympathetics: Frey syndrome after parotidectomy is gustatory sweating from misdirected parotid parasympathetic fibers (lesser petrosal pathway) growing into sweat-gland sympathetic territory, and a glomus tympanicum paraganglioma arises on the promontory along this plexus, giving pulsatile tinnitus and a red retrotympanic mass.

name: Cervical cardiac nerves (sympathetic) and cervical cardiac branches of vagus
function: Autonomic nerves that descend from the neck into the thorax to form the cardiac plexus: superior, middle and inferior cervical cardiac nerves from the three cervical sympathetic ganglia, and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches from the vagus.

details.label: Type
details.value: Sympathetic: postganglionic from the superior, middle and cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglia (preganglionic cell bodies T1-T4/5), plus visceral afferents for cardiac pain. Vagal: preganglionic parasympathetic and visceral afferents

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Sympathetic cardiac nerves descend behind the carotid sheath and in front of or beside the subclavian artery into the superior mediastinum; the vagal cardiac branches leave the vagus in the neck (superior) and near the recurrent laryngeal nerve at the root of the neck (inferior)

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Cardiac plexus (superficial and deep) on the aortic arch and tracheal bifurcation: sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, myocardium and coronary arteries. Sympathetic fibers increase rate, conduction and contractility; vagal fibers slow rate and AV conduction

details.label: Branches
details.value: Superior, middle and inferior cervical cardiac nerves; superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches of the vagus; thoracic cardiac branches below

pearl: Cardiac pain afferents run with the sympathetic cardiac nerves to T1-T5, so angina refers to the left arm and jaw and the vagal afferents that go with the superior cardiac branch can give the epigastric/neck pain of an inferior MI. Left stellate ganglion block or cardiac sympathetic denervation treats refractory ventricular arrhythmia and long-QT syndrome; vagal cardiac branches are the efferent limb of carotid sinus massage and the Valsalva maneuver.

name: Superior and inferior ganglia of CN IX and CN X
function: Sensory ganglia on the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves at the jugular foramen: a small superior ganglion of each inside the foramen and a larger inferior ganglion just below it (the petrosal ganglion of IX, the nodose ganglion of X).

details.label: Type
details.value: Pseudounipolar sensory cell bodies: general somatic sensory (superior ganglia; ear and meninges), visceral sensory and taste (inferior ganglia). No synapses occur here

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Both nerves pass through the middle (pars vascularis/nervosa) compartment of the jugular foramen with CN XI; the superior ganglia lie within the foramen, the inferior ganglia 1-2 cm below it in front of the internal jugular vein

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Inferior ganglion of IX: carotid sinus and body, pharynx, tonsil, posterior 1/3 tongue taste, middle ear (tympanic nerve). Inferior ganglion of X: pharynx, larynx (superior laryngeal nerve), thoracic and abdominal viscera, taste from the epiglottis. Superior ganglia: auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold) and the meningeal branches to the posterior fossa dura

details.label: Branches
details.value: From the ganglia or just beyond them: tympanic nerve (IX), carotid sinus nerve (IX), meningeal and auricular branches (X), pharyngeal branch and superior laryngeal nerve (X); communications between IX, X and the superior cervical ganglion

pearl: Central processes of these ganglia end in the nucleus of the solitary tract (visceral/taste) and spinal trigeminal nucleus (somatic), which is why ear pain is a referred symptom of pharyngeal and laryngeal cancer and why coughing on ear-canal stimulation (Arnold reflex) occurs. A glomus jugulare paraganglioma or jugular foramen tumor compressing the ganglia produces the jugular foramen (Vernet) syndrome: loss of gag and posterior-tongue taste, dysphagia, hoarseness and ipsilateral palate droop, with CN XI weakness.

name: Meningeal branch of mandibular nerve (nervus spinosus)
function: Recurrent sensory branch of the mandibular nerve that re-enters the skull through the foramen spinosum with the middle meningeal artery to supply the dura of the middle cranial fossa and the mastoid air cells.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory (with sympathetic fibers from the middle meningeal plexus)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Arises from the trunk of V3 just below the foramen ovale -> ascends through the foramen spinosum with the middle meningeal artery and veins -> divides with the frontal and parietal branches of the artery

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Dura mater of the middle cranial fossa and the lateral convexity along the middle meningeal artery; mucosa of the mastoid air cells (posterior branch); the dura of the anterior fossa is supplied by V1 (tentorial/ethmoidal) and the posterior fossa by C2-C3 and CN X

details.label: Branches
details.value: Anterior branch with the frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery, posterior branch with the parietal branch

pearl: Dural pain is carried by trigeminal meningeal branches, so supratentorial dural irritation (meningitis, epidural hematoma stretching the dura, dural traction in low-pressure headache) presents as frontotemporal headache in V1-V3 territory, whereas posterior fossa lesions give occipital and neck pain; the brain parenchyma itself is insensate.

name: Nerve to subclavius (C5-C6)
function: Small motor branch of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus that descends in front of the plexus and the subclavian vessels to supply the subclavius muscle; it often gives an accessory phrenic nerve.

details.label: Type
details.value: Somatic motor (C5, C6); carries proprioceptive fibers

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Leaves the anterior surface of the upper trunk (or the C5-C6 junction) in the posterior triangle -> descends in front of the subclavian artery and the 3rd part of the plexus, behind the clavicle -> enters the superior surface of subclavius

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Subclavius (from the 1st rib and its cartilage to the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle), which anchors and depresses the clavicle (Netter Muscle Table 2.8)

details.label: Branches
details.value: Accessory phrenic nerve (in up to half of people) that joins the phrenic nerve in front of the subclavian vein, carrying C5 fibers to the diaphragm

pearl: The subclavius and its nerve lie directly behind the middle third of the clavicle and cushion the subclavian vessels and plexus in a midshaft clavicle fracture. Because the accessory phrenic nerve usually passes in front of the subclavian vein, it can be injured during subclavian central line placement or first-rib resection, and a phrenic block at the C5 root level may miss it, leaving residual diaphragm function.

name: Sensory root of trigeminal nerve
function: Large root of CN V that carries the central processes of trigeminal ganglion neurons into the lateral pons, conveying all touch, pain and temperature from the face, mouth, nose and dura.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory (central processes of trigeminal ganglion cells; proprioceptive fibers pass through to the mesencephalic nucleus)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Lateral surface of the pons -> over the petrous apex beneath the superior petrosal sinus -> trigeminal ganglion in the trigeminal (Meckel) cave

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Fibers of V1, V2 and V3 ending in the principal sensory nucleus (touch) and the spinal tract and nucleus (pain, temperature)

details.label: Branches
details.value: None; continuous peripherally with the trigeminal ganglion and its three divisions

pearl: Trigeminal neuralgia is usually compression of this root at its pontine entry zone by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery; treat with carbamazepine, then microvascular decompression. In a young patient or bilateral cases think multiple sclerosis.

name: Motor root of trigeminal nerve
function: Small root of CN V from the motor nucleus in the pons that passes beneath the trigeminal ganglion without synapsing and joins the mandibular nerve at the foramen ovale to supply the first-arch muscles.

details.label: Type
details.value: Branchial motor (first pharyngeal arch)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Leaves the pons anteromedial to the sensory root -> runs deep (inferior) to the trigeminal ganglion -> foramen ovale, where it joins the sensory part of V3

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, tensor tympani

details.label: Branches
details.value: Distributed only through the mandibular nerve (V3)

pearl: A lesion makes the jaw deviate toward the weak side on opening with wasting of masseter and temporalis; the motor nucleus receives bilateral corticobulbar input, so a unilateral stroke above it causes little weakness.

name: Anterior division of mandibular nerve (V3)
function: Smaller, mainly motor division of V3 formed just below the foramen ovale; it supplies three muscles of mastication and gives the sensory buccal nerve.

details.label: Type
details.value: Mainly branchial motor, with one sensory branch (buccal nerve)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Arises in the infratemporal fossa below the foramen ovale, deep to the lateral pterygoid; its branches pass above or between the heads of that muscle

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Masseter, temporalis, lateral pterygoid; skin and mucosa of the cheek and buccal gingiva of the mandibular molars

details.label: Branches
details.value: Masseteric nerve, deep temporal nerves (anterior and posterior), nerve to lateral pterygoid, buccal nerve

pearl: Remember the anterior division as motor except the buccal nerve, and the posterior division as sensory except the nerve to mylohyoid; the buccal nerve must be blocked separately for work on the lower molars.

name: Posterior division of mandibular nerve (V3)
function: Larger, mainly sensory division of V3 that descends deep to the lateral pterygoid and splits into the auriculotemporal, lingual and inferior alveolar nerves.

details.label: Type
details.value: Mainly general sensory, with motor fibers in the nerve to mylohyoid

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Arises below the foramen ovale and runs down medial to the lateral pterygoid; the auriculotemporal nerve turns back around the middle meningeal artery, the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves emerge at the lower border of the lateral pterygoid

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Temple, auricle, external acoustic meatus and TMJ; anterior 2/3 of tongue and floor of mouth; mandibular teeth, chin and lower lip; mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric

details.label: Branches
details.value: Auriculotemporal nerve, lingual nerve (joined by the chorda tympani), inferior alveolar nerve (gives the nerve to mylohyoid, then the mental nerve and incisive branch)

pearl: An inferior alveolar nerve block at the mandibular foramen also numbs the adjacent lingual nerve (half of the tongue); both nerves are at risk in third-molar extraction.

name: Superior division of oculomotor nerve
function: Smaller upper branch of CN III, formed as the nerve enters the superior orbital fissure; it supplies the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris.

details.label: Type
details.value: Somatic motor

details.label: Exit foramen
details.value: Superior orbital fissure, inside the common tendinous ring

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Superior rectus, levator palpebrae superioris

details.label: Branches
details.value: Muscular branches entering the deep surface of superior rectus and passing through or around it to the levator

pearl: An isolated superior-division palsy gives ptosis with impaired elevation and a normal pupil; with a lesion at the superior orbital fissure or anterior cavernous sinus, look for a mass or aneurysm.

name: Inferior division of oculomotor nerve
function: Larger lower branch of CN III that supplies the medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique and carries the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the ciliary ganglion.

details.label: Type
details.value: Somatic motor + parasympathetic (from the accessory oculomotor [Edinger-Westphal] nucleus)

details.label: Exit foramen
details.value: Superior orbital fissure, inside the common tendinous ring

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique; sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle via the ciliary ganglion

details.label: Branches
details.value: Branches to medial and inferior rectus, long branch to inferior oblique, parasympathetic root of the ciliary ganglion (from the branch to inferior oblique)

pearl: An inferior-division palsy gives impaired adduction and depression with a dilated, poorly reactive pupil but no ptosis.

name: Vestibular nerve
function: Balance part of CN VIII: bipolar neurons of the vestibular ganglion in the internal acoustic meatus carry head-position and head-movement signals from the maculae and ampullary crests to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.

details.label: Type
details.value: Special sensory (equilibrium)

details.label: Exit foramen
details.value: Internal acoustic meatus (superior and inferior vestibular areas of the fundus) -> cerebellopontine angle

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Utricle and saccule (linear acceleration, gravity); ampullae of the three semicircular ducts (angular acceleration); central fibers to the superior, inferior, medial and lateral vestibular nuclei and via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the cerebellum

details.label: Branches
details.value: See divisions; also gives efferent fibers that join the cochlear nerve in the meatus

details.label: Divisions
details.value: Superior division: utricle and ampullae of the superior (anterior) and lateral semicircular ducts. Inferior division: saccule and ampulla of the posterior semicircular duct. Vestibular ganglion lies on the nerve in the internal acoustic meatus

pearl: Vestibular neuritis: acute sustained vertigo with horizontal nystagmus, a positive head-impulse test and normal hearing. Vestibular schwannoma arises from this nerve but presents with unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus from cochlear nerve compression.

name: Cochlear nerve
function: Hearing part of CN VIII: bipolar neurons of the cochlear (spiral) ganglion in the modiolus carry signals from the hair cells of the spiral organ to the cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction.

details.label: Type
details.value: Special sensory (hearing); also contains efferent fibers to the sensory epithelium that reach it from the vestibular nerve

details.label: Exit foramen
details.value: Modiolus of the cochlea -> internal acoustic meatus (anteroinferior quadrant) -> cerebellopontine angle

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Spiral organ (of Corti); central fibers end in the anterior and posterior cochlear nuclei on the inferior cerebellar peduncle

details.label: Branches
details.value: None; joins the vestibular nerve to form CN VIII

pearl: A lesion gives ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss (Weber lateralizes away, Rinne air > bone); beyond the cochlear nuclei the pathway is bilateral, so central lesions do not cause unilateral deafness.

name: Temporofacial division of facial nerve
function: Upper of the two divisions into which the facial nerve trunk splits inside the parotid gland; it gives the temporal and zygomatic branches and contributes to the buccal branches.

details.label: Type
details.value: Branchial motor (second pharyngeal arch)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Forms at the pes anserinus in the parotid gland, superficial to the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery, and runs up and forward

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Frontal belly of occipitofrontalis, orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii, zygomaticus muscles and other muscles above the mouth

details.label: Branches
details.value: Temporal branches, zygomatic branches, upper buccal branches

pearl: The facial nerve plane separates the superficial and deep parts of the parotid; in superficial parotidectomy the trunk is found first and each division is followed forward to avoid facial weakness.

name: Cervicofacial division of facial nerve
function: Lower of the two divisions of the facial nerve trunk inside the parotid gland; it gives buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.

details.label: Type
details.value: Branchial motor (second pharyngeal arch)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Forms at the pes anserinus in the parotid gland and runs down and forward toward the angle of the mandible

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Buccinator, orbicularis oris, depressors of the lower lip and angle of the mouth, mentalis, platysma

details.label: Branches
details.value: Lower buccal branches, marginal mandibular branch, cervical branch

pearl: Its marginal mandibular branch has few cross-connections, so injury during submandibular or neck surgery leaves a lasting asymmetric lower lip.

name: Digastric and stylohyoid branches of facial nerve
function: Short motor branches given off by the facial nerve just below the stylomastoid foramen, before it enters the parotid, to the posterior belly of digastric and the stylohyoid.

details.label: Type
details.value: Branchial motor (second pharyngeal arch)

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Arise from the trunk immediately after the stylomastoid foramen, often by a common stem, and run down to the muscles

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Posterior belly of digastric, stylohyoid

details.label: Branches
details.value: Digastric branch, stylohyoid branch

pearl: The posterior belly of digastric is the surgical landmark for the facial nerve trunk, which lies just deep and superior to its upper border; the anterior belly is supplied by V3, reflecting its first-arch origin.

name: Cranial root of accessory nerve
function: Rootlets from the caudal nucleus ambiguus that briefly join the accessory nerve at the jugular foramen and then pass to the vagus, which distributes them to the muscles of the soft palate, pharynx and larynx.

details.label: Type
details.value: Branchial motor (functionally part of the vagus)

details.label: Exit foramen
details.value: Jugular foramen; leaves the lateral medulla below the vagal rootlets

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Via the pharyngeal and laryngeal branches of the vagus: muscles of the palate (except tensor veli palatini), pharynx (except stylopharyngeus) and larynx

details.label: Branches
details.value: Joins the vagus at its inferior ganglion (internal branch of the accessory nerve)

pearl: Because these fibers travel with the vagus, a jugular foramen lesion gives palatal droop, dysphagia and hoarseness together with sternocleidomastoid and trapezius weakness.

name: Spinal root of accessory nerve
function: Root from the accessory nucleus of the upper cervical cord (C1-C5) that ascends through the foramen magnum and leaves the skull through the jugular foramen as the accessory nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

details.label: Type
details.value: Motor (proprioceptive fibers join from C2-C4 of the cervical plexus)

details.label: Exit foramen
details.value: Enters the skull through the foramen magnum, exits through the jugular foramen

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Sternocleidomastoid, trapezius

details.label: Branches
details.value: Rootlets emerge between the anterior and posterior spinal roots, behind the denticulate ligament; after the jugular foramen it continues as the accessory nerve (external branch)

pearl: It is the nerve at risk in the posterior triangle: lymph node biopsy there causes shoulder droop and weak abduction above the horizontal with a spared sternocleidomastoid.

name: Vertebral ganglion
function: Small inconstant ganglion of the cervical sympathetic trunk lying in front of the vertebral artery near its origin, between the middle cervical and cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglia.

details.label: Type
details.value: Sympathetic chain ganglion (postganglionic cell bodies)

details.label: Location
details.value: Anterior to the vertebral artery just before it enters the C6 transverse foramen, at about C7

details.label: Branches
details.value: Contributes to the vertebral plexus and to gray rami; gives origin to the ansa subclavia

details.label: Connections
details.value: Middle cervical ganglion above; cervicothoracic ganglion below by trunk fibers passing in front of and behind the vertebral artery and by the ansa subclavia

name: Ansa subclavia
function: Loop of the cervical sympathetic trunk that passes in front of and under the first part of the subclavian artery, connecting the middle cervical (or vertebral) ganglion with the cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion.

details.label: Type
details.value: Sympathetic interganglionic loop

details.label: Location
details.value: Around the first part of the subclavian artery, medial to the internal thoracic artery origin and on the cervical pleura

details.label: Branches
details.value: Twigs to the subclavian artery plexus; communicates with the phrenic nerve

details.label: Connections
details.value: Middle cervical/vertebral ganglion above, cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion below

pearl: Surgery or trauma at the thoracic inlet around the subclavian artery can damage the loop and adjacent stellate ganglion, producing Horner syndrome.

name: Zygomaticotemporal nerve
function: Terminal branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) that passes through the zygomatic bone into the temporal fossa to supply the skin of the anterior temple.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory; carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion to the lacrimal nerve

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Lateral wall of the orbit -> zygomaticotemporal foramen -> temporal fossa -> pierces the temporal fascia about 2 cm above the zygomatic arch

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Skin of the anterior temple (non-hair-bearing)

details.label: Branches
details.value: Communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve (secretomotor to the lacrimal gland)

pearl: It is a recognised trigger site in temple migraine surgery and is the route by which lacrimal secretomotor fibers reach the gland, so a pterygopalatine ganglion lesion gives a dry eye.

name: Zygomaticofacial nerve
function: Terminal branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) that emerges on the face through the zygomaticofacial foramen to supply the skin over the prominence of the cheek.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Inferolateral orbit -> zygomaticofacial foramen on the lateral surface of the zygomatic bone -> pierces orbicularis oculi

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Skin over the zygomatic prominence (malar eminence)

details.label: Branches
details.value: Communicates with zygomatic branches of the facial nerve and palpebral branches of V2

pearl: Numbness over the cheek prominence after a zygomatic (tripod) fracture reflects injury to this nerve and the infraorbital nerve.

name: External nasal branch of anterior ethmoidal nerve
function: Terminal cutaneous branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (nasociliary, V1) that emerges between the nasal bone and the lateral nasal cartilage to supply the skin of the dorsum and tip of the nose.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory

details.label: Exit/route
details.value: Runs in a groove on the deep surface of the nasal bone and emerges at its lower border, between it and the lateral nasal cartilage

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Skin of the dorsum, ala and tip of the nose

details.label: Branches
details.value: Terminal twigs only; it is the continuation of the anterior ethmoidal nerve after the internal nasal branches

pearl: Hutchinson sign: zoster vesicles on the tip of the nose mean nasociliary involvement and a high risk of ocular disease, so refer urgently to ophthalmology.

name: Posterior cutaneous branches of posterior rami of C4-C8
function: Segmental cutaneous nerves from the medial branches of the lower cervical posterior rami that pierce semispinalis, splenius and trapezius near the midline to supply the skin of the back of the neck.

details.label: Type
details.value: General sensory (terminal cutaneous twigs of mixed posterior rami)

details.label: Route
details.value: Medial branches of the posterior rami pass back around the articular pillars, supply the deep muscles and facet joints, then pierce trapezius close to the spinous processes

details.label: Supplies
details.value: Skin of the posterior neck below the territory of the third occipital nerve; C4-C6 are the main contributors, C7 and C8 are minimal

details.label: Root
details.value: Posterior rami of C4-C8 (medial branches)

pearl: The same medial branches supply the cervical facet joints, which is why medial branch blocks and radiofrequency ablation are used for facet-mediated neck pain.
